🌍 IRGC chief calls Hormuz security ‘a red line,’ warns enemies against interference

📌 Tehran, IRNA - The commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolution Guards Corps (IRGC) warns that the security of the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz is “a red line” for the Islamic Republic, and that no extra-regional power can threaten, dominate, or interfere in the strategic waterway.

In a message marking IRGC Navy Day on Thursday, Major General Ahmad Vahidi said the IRGC Navy had forced an “aggressor fleet” to retreat from the Persian Gulf by blocking, managing, and controlling the Strait of Hormuz.
​
The IRGC chief described the waterway as “the vital artery of global energy and the strategic red line of Islamic Iran.”
​
Gen. Vahidi said the naval forces under his command had completed its “calendar of honors with courage and martyrdom” during the third American-Zionist imposed war, and warned that any threat would be met with a decisive response.
​
He said the IRGC Navy, in close coordination with the Iranian Army Navy, is equipped with precision-guided missiles, offensive drones, fast attack vessels, electronic warfare capabilities, and a coastal defense network, and is prepared to respond to any “miscalculation” by the enemy regarding unauthorized transits through waters under its management.
​
The general said the IRGC Navy’s strategy is “clear, principled, and unchangeable,” adding that protecting the Strait of Hormuz amounts to protecting Iran’s national interests, the security of the nation, and the country’s dignity.
​
He also paid tribute to Nader Mahdavi, an IRGC naval commander whose martyrdom on October 8, 1987 is commemorated on IRGC Navy Day, and to IRGC naval commanders Alireza Tangsiri and Behnam Rezaei.
​
Gen. Vahidi concluded by urging IRGC naval personnel to remain ready to defend Iran and the Strait of Hormuz “at any time and in any arena,” under the command of Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Sayyid Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei.

“Naza” is an Israeli military term referring to the number of civilians expected to be killed in airstrikes.

Israeli intelligence officers revealed that during the first weeks of the war on Gaza, the military permitted the killing of 15 to 20 civilians to target a low-ranking Hamas member, and more than 100 to target a commander. Some targets were reportedly reviewed in just 20 seconds, with strikes often carried out on homes at night.

In the documentary “Naza,” an officer revealed that the permitted civilian death toll for a single strike once reached 500.

Although Israel’s military chief claimed in January 2025 that 20,000 fighters had been killed, an Israeli military database reportedly contained around 8,900 names in May, compared with 53,000 deaths recorded by Gaza’s Health Ministry — roughly one in six, according to this comparison.

The Israeli military rejected the documentary’s allegations, insisting that each strike is individually assessed to prevent excessive civilian harm.

The question remains: Who decides how many civilian deaths are considered “excessive”?
